title: Season passes
brief: Write a planning analysis for a fictional community cinema choosing whether to expand its annual pass. Four pilot months, Jan through Apr. Passes active: 80, 95, 105, 112. Pass-holder visits: 180, 250, 205, 280. Single tickets sold: 940, 880, 1020, 865. Available seats: 2000, 1840, 2100, 1750. Single ticket 9 currency units; annual pass 100; each visit incurs a 2-unit screening royalty. Some screenings sold out but the times were not recorded. A volunteer survey suggests pass holders bring friends. Capacity is uneven across nights and programming changed monthly. Analyze what can and cannot be inferred from this pilot. The board needs a proposal for the next season.

ed4434f3b635ab20.text:
# Annual Pass Pilot: What the Evidence Supports and a Proposal for Next Season

## Recommendation

The board should continue the annual pass next season and allow it to grow to a hard cap of 200 passes, but should not approve open-ended expansion. The pilot shows the pass covers its direct costs and has not visibly harmed single-ticket sales. It does not show whether the pass adds income or merely discounts tickets that would have been bought anyway. That question decides whether expansion is worthwhile, and the pilot was not set up to answer it. Next season should be run so that it does.

## What the pilot recorded

| | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Passes active | 80 | 95 | 105 | 112 | n/a |
| Pass-holder visits | 180 | 250 | 205 | 280 | 915 |
| Single tickets | 940 | 880 | 1,020 | 865 | 3,705 |
| Available seats | 2,000 | 1,840 | 2,100 | 1,750 | 7,690 |
| Occupancy | 56.0% | 61.4% | 58.3% | 65.4% | 60.1% |
| Visits per active pass | 2.25 | 2.63 | 1.95 | 2.50 | 2.33 |
| Pass share of admissions | 16.1% | 22.1% | 16.7% | 24.5% | 19.8% |
| Single tickets per seat | 47.0% | 47.8% | 48.6% | 49.4% | 48.2% |

The financial figures assume that "passes active" means passes sold to date at the full price of 100, and that the 2-unit royalty applies to every admission, including pass visits.

- **Single tickets:** revenue of 33,345, less 7,410 in royalties, gives a contribution of 25,935.
- **Passes, cash basis:** 112 passes brought in 11,200. Most of this pays for visits not yet made.
- **Passes, earned basis:** spreading each pass over twelve months, the 392 pass-months to date earned about 3,267. Royalties on pass visits were 1,830, leaving a contribution of about 1,437.
- **Yield per visit:** a pass visit earns about 3.57 before royalty and 1.57 after. A single ticket earns 9 and 7.

Pass holders therefore account for about 20% of admissions and about 9% of earned revenue.

## What can be inferred

**The pass covers its royalties at current usage.** At 2.33 visits a month, a holder makes about 28 visits a year, costing 56 in royalties against the 100 price. The pass only falls below royalty cost at 50 visits a year, or more than four a month. No month came close to that on average.

**Average occupancy leaves room.** With 40% of seats empty overall, most pass visits filled seats that would otherwise have been unsold.

**Single-ticket sales did not fall relative to capacity.** Raw single-ticket sales moved up and down, but they tracked the number of seats offered. Single tickets per available seat rose slightly each month, from 47.0% to 49.4%, while passes grew by 40%. This is the most encouraging pattern in the data. It rules out heavy, obvious cannibalisation, though not the moderate kind discussed below.

**Sign-ups are slowing.** Net additions were 15, 10 and 7 in successive months. At the current price and level of promotion, demand appears to be levelling off, so a cap of 200 is unlikely to be reached without active selling.

## What cannot be inferred

**Whether pass holders would have bought tickets anyway.** This is the central unknown. The pilot has no record of what holders bought before they held a pass. The steady single-ticket rate per seat is only four data points, and programming changed every month, so a stronger programme could easily mask lost sales.

**How many friends pass holders bring.** The volunteer survey says holders bring friends. It gives no number, relies on self-report, and cannot show whether those friends would have come anyway. It supports the idea but cannot be entered into a budget.

**How many paying customers were turned away.** Some screenings sold out, but the times were not recorded, and neither were turn-aways. A pass holder occupying a seat that a single-ticket buyer wanted costs the cinema 9 units. Capacity is uneven across nights, so a 60% monthly average is compatible with regular full houses on the popular nights. Those are the nights pass holders are most likely to choose.

**Annual usage.** The figure of 28 visits a year extrapolates from four months, January to April. Usage may differ in summer, and it may fade as the novelty of the pass wears off. Early buyers are also likely to be the keenest attenders, so later buyers may visit less.

**The spread of usage across holders.** Only monthly totals were kept. An average of 2.33 could mean most holders come twice a month, or that a few come weekly while many rarely come. These have different implications for pricing and for seat pressure.

**Renewal.** No pass has reached its anniversary. The pilot says nothing about whether holders will pay again.

**The effect of programming.** Pass visits were highest in February and April, the two months with the fewest seats. That could reflect the films shown, the schedule, or chance. With four months and a different programme in each, these cannot be separated.

## What the unknowns are worth

The incremental value of one pass over a year can be written as:

**100 − (2 × pass visits) − (7 × single tickets the holder would otherwise have bought) + (7 × extra friend tickets) − (9 × paying customers displaced)**

At 28 visits a year, the first two terms come to 44. The pass therefore breaks even against the alternative of no pass if the holder would otherwise have bought about six single tickets a year, roughly one every two months. Each genuinely additional friend ticket offsets one lost ticket.

| Type of holder | Tickets otherwise bought | Extra friend tickets | Customers displaced | Net effect per pass per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Occasional visitor | 2 | 0 | 0 | +30 |
| Regular | 6 | 0 | 0 | +2 |
| Regular, some sold-out visits | 6 | 0 | 3 | −25 |
| Enthusiast | 12 | 0 | 0 | −40 |
| Enthusiast who brings friends | 12 | 4 | 0 | −12 |

These rows are illustrations, not estimates. They show that the answer turns on who buys the pass. Someone who already came monthly gets a large discount at the cinema's expense. Someone who came twice a year becomes a better customer.

Displacement matters on the same scale. If one pass visit in ten during the pilot took a seat from a paying customer, the cost would have been about 820 units, more than half of the pass's earned contribution for the period.

Scaled up, the exposure is bounded. If the four pilot months are typical, single tickets contribute roughly 78,000 a year. At 200 passes, the scenarios above range from about +6,000 if every holder is an occasional visitor to about −8,000 if every holder is an enthusiast. The realistic outcome lies between these. The pass is therefore unlikely to change the cinema's finances by more than about a tenth in either direction. A capped expansion at that level of risk is acceptable as a way of finding out, but selling without limit is not.

## Proposal for next season

**1. Cap the scheme at 200 passes.** This includes renewals of the existing 112. It allows meaningful growth, keeps the worst case within the range above, and gives a large enough group to measure.

**2. Hold the price at 100.** Changing the price at the same time as collecting the first usable data would make the results harder to read. The price should be reviewed at the mid-season checkpoint with evidence in hand.

**3. Require pass holders to book, and limit pass bookings to 25% of seats per screening in advance.** Unsold seats are released to pass holders on the day. Pass holders averaged 20% of admissions and reached about 25% in the busiest month, so this limit would rarely be felt on ordinary nights. It would bind only where demand is strong, which is where displacement occurs.

**4. Record what the pilot did not.** None of this needs new equipment, only a consistent log at the box office.

- **Per screening:** seats available, single tickets sold, pass admissions, the time the screening sold out, and the number of people turned away.
- **Per pass visit:** the pass number, so that visits per holder can be counted.
- **Per pass transaction:** the number of single tickets bought alongside it, as a direct measure of friends brought.
- **At purchase or renewal:** one question on how often the buyer attended in the previous twelve months. This is self-reported and imperfect, but it is the only available evidence on prior buying.

**5. Set a mid-season review with stated tests.** After six months the board should look at four measures.

| Measure | Signal to expand | Signal to restrict or reprice |
|---|---|---|
| Typical prior attendance of holders | Under 6 visits a year | Over 6 visits a year, without matching friend tickets |
| Friend tickets per pass per year | Enough to cover any shortfall above | Negligible |
| Turn-aways at screenings with pass admissions | Rare | Frequent despite the 25% limit |
| Visits per pass per year | Well under 50 | Approaching 50 |

If the signals favour expansion, the cap can be lifted for the following season. If they do not, the options are a higher price, a pass valid only on off-peak nights, or a limit on visits. The data will show which of these fits the problem.

**6. Report pass income on an earned basis.** Cash from pass sales arrives up front and can make the scheme look stronger than it is. Board reports should show one-twelfth of each pass per month against that month's royalties, with the cash figure shown separately.

## Decision requested

The board is asked to approve:

- continuation of the annual pass at 100 units, capped at 200 passes;
- advance booking for pass holders with a 25% per-screening limit;
- the record-keeping set out in item 4;
- a review at six months against the tests in item 5.

18335f014450e082.text:
# Annual pass proposal for the next season

The board should retain the 100-unit annual pass and authorize a staged expansion. The pilot shows that pass holders used the cinema regularly and that the cinema had spare seats in every month. It also records sold-out screenings. Both facts matter. An extra pass holder who attends a quiet screening can bring in subscription income at little additional cost. An extra pass holder who would otherwise buy single tickets, or who takes the last seat a single-ticket customer wanted, can reduce the money available for programming. The pilot establishes how often members attended in aggregate. It leaves open which of those circumstances was most common.

For next season, the cinema should offer renewals and release an initial batch of up to 20 additional passes. That batch would generate up to 2,000 units in gross receipts and expand the active base by about 18% relative to April if all 112 passes remain active. Twenty is a proposed trial size the board can review after one quarter. The evidence does not establish an optimal membership ceiling. The board should reserve a second batch of up to 20 for a separate decision, informed by screening-level demand, the purchasing history of new members where available, and an estimate of the cost of honoring their passes for a full year.

## What happened during the pilot

| Month | Active passes | Pass-holder visits | Visits per active pass | Single tickets | Total visits | Available seats | Occupancy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan | 80 | 180 | 2.25 | 940 | 1,120 | 2,000 | 56.0% |
| Feb | 95 | 250 | 2.63 | 880 | 1,130 | 1,840 | 61.4% |
| Mar | 105 | 205 | 1.95 | 1,020 | 1,225 | 2,100 | 58.3% |
| Apr | 112 | 280 | 2.50 | 865 | 1,145 | 1,750 | 65.4% |
| **Pilot total** | **—** | **915** | **2.33** | **3,705** | **4,620** | **7,690** | **60.1%** |

Active passes rose from 80 to 112, a 40% increase. Pass holders accounted for nearly one visit in five across the pilot. The average of 2.33 visits per active pass per month uses 392 active pass-months, the sum of the four monthly counts. A person with an active pass throughout contributes four pass-months. These figures tell the board how much attendance the membership base generated, but they cannot distinguish broad participation from a pattern in which a few frequent visitors accounted for much of the use. The increase of 32 active passes is also a net change. Without issue and expiry dates, the cinema cannot reconstruct gross sales, renewals, or cash receipts from those counts.

April illustrates why the choice of measure matters. It had the highest occupancy and the most pass visits, yet March drew 80 more visits overall. April offered 350 fewer seats. February and April combined relatively high pass use with lower single-ticket sales, which could suggest that some people switched from tickets to passes. Monthly changes in films, screening schedules, and seat supply could produce the same pattern. Four months with different programs provide no reliable estimate of how many single tickets the cinema would have sold without the pass.

## What the seats and receipts can tell the board

Across the pilot, 3,070 seats went unused. That makes it plausible that the cinema could welcome more members at some performances. It gives little guidance about a particular Friday evening. A vacant seat on Tuesday cannot accommodate someone turned away on Friday, and moving a member to Tuesday only helps if that person wants to see the film then. Because the sold-out screening times were not recorded, the board cannot tell whether scarcity was concentrated in one popular title, recurred on the same night each week, or affected screenings with substantial pass use. Even a sellout with many members present would not by itself establish lost ticket sales. That requires evidence that someone else wanted a seat.

The financial records support a partial calculation. Single tickets generated 33,345 units. The 4,620 visits incurred 9,240 units in royalties, including 1,830 for pass-holder visits. This leaves 24,105 units from single-ticket receipts after the royalties on **all** visits, before pass income and other operating costs. It is a useful subtotal for reconciling the pilot accounts. Adding 100 units for every active pass each month would count the same annual entitlement repeatedly. Even a complete record of pass sales during the pilot would need to be read alongside the remaining months of access the cinema owes each buyer.

The economics of one annual pass show which missing evidence matters most. Suppose a new member makes 28 visits over the year, roughly the result of extending the pilot’s average monthly use across 12 months. That is a planning scenario, since summer programming, seasonal attendance, and the habits of new buyers may differ. The pass brings in 100 units and those visits incur 56 in royalties. If every visit is additional and there is room for everyone who wants to attend, 44 units remain before other costs. Under those assumptions, 50 visits would use the entire pass price in royalties.

Now suppose the same member would have bought seven single tickets without the pass. Those tickets would have contributed 49 units after royalties. The pass still contributes 44 units on its own, but the cinema ends up **5 units worse off** than it would have been selling the seven tickets. If a different customer also loses a seat they would have bought, the cinema forgoes a further 7 units of ticket contribution, assuming that customer never rebooks. This distinction matters when evaluating crowded shows. A customer who switches to another performance and buys a ticket there presents a service concern, while a customer who abandons the purchase also represents lost income.

The volunteer survey suggests a possible benefit on the other side of the calculation. If a member brings a friend who buys a 9-unit ticket, would otherwise have stayed home, and uses an available seat, the cinema gains 7 units after the royalty. That one visit would cover the 5-unit shortfall in the seven-ticket example. The survey gives the board a reason to investigate this effect. It supplies neither the number of paying guests nor evidence about what they would otherwise have done. Counting every companion as new business would overstate the case for expansion, particularly if friends already attended together before one bought a pass.

## How to run the expansion

Keep the price and existing booking terms for the first batch. Changing the price, membership limit, and access rules together would leave the board guessing which change affected demand. Offer the places through the cinema’s usual public channels and record applications beyond the cap on a waiting list. Track renewals separately. If many existing members leave, selling 20 new passes may largely replace that loss. The board should see the number of active passes alongside gross sales and the size of the waiting list.

Give the box office one screening record it can complete as part of closing each performance. Record the title, date, start time, seats offered for sale, single tickets sold, pass reservations, actual admissions by ticket type, and whether and when booking closed because the show was full. For sold-out shows, record waiting-list requests or observed turnaways and, where practical, whether those customers obtained a seat at a later performance. A reservation count alone can make a show appear full even when no-shows leave seats empty. Recording both bookings and admissions would help the cinema decide whether a reservation-release rule could recover seats before it considers limiting member access.

At enrollment, ask new members how many single tickets they bought in the previous year and whether they expect to visit more often with the pass. Where members agree and records exist, use their actual prior purchases to check the estimates. Track visits by pass and issue date so a person who joined late in the quarter is compared with others who had similar time to attend. A short, optional guest question at selected performances can establish whether a paying visitor came with a member and whether they expect they would have attended anyway. Report the number of responses as well as the answers. A handful of enthusiastic respondents should carry correspondingly little weight in the financial forecast.

The programming team can use these records before the quarter ends. If one title repeatedly sells out while another performance of the same film has space, tell members and other customers about the available showing when they book. If demand exceeds capacity across all showings of a title, an extra performance may be worth considering against its staffing and operating costs. Compare similar titles and time slots when judging the result. A quieter audience after a blockbuster leaves the schedule says little about whether an intervention worked.

## The decision after one quarter

Before releasing the second batch, the board should review a full-year contribution forecast for the first 20 new passes, with higher-use and lower-use cases. Start with actual pass receipts, deduct projected royalties on member visits, deduct the contribution from single tickets members would likely have purchased, and allow for other paying customers who lost sales at full performances. Add the contribution from plausibly additional paying guests and deduct any extra operating costs. Show a case with no guest benefit so the board can see whether the financial decision depends on an effect the survey has yet to establish. Keep assumptions visible, especially where one more former ticket purchase per member would change the decision.

Release the second batch if the forecast remains positive under a reasonable cautious case and screening records show that the cinema can accommodate the added demand without recurring turnaways at popular performances. Hold at the first batch if the financial result depends on optimistic guest assumptions or if the same time slots repeatedly leave customers without seats. Where the quarter contains too few comparable screenings to judge, keep collecting records through the next programming cycle. Honor the annual terms already sold throughout that review.

The board may also decide that affordable repeat attendance merits a modest subsidy. In that case, it should name the amount it is prepared to spend and assess whether the pass reaches the people it hopes to serve. That gives the cinema two defensible grounds for expansion: a pass that helps pay for the program, or an explicitly funded access benefit. The staged proposal lets the board pursue either purpose while learning where seats are available, who gains access, and what the annual commitment costs.

263bc2ad27455f2e.text:
# Annual pass expansion proposal

The cinema should expand the annual pass next season through a limited release, with further sales contingent on screening-level capacity and the financial performance of each group of buyers. The pilot shows that pass holders used the cinema regularly and that recorded admissions filled about 60% of available seats across four months. Some screenings still sold out, and the cinema lacks the showtime records needed to know where additional pass use would fit. A limited release gives the board a way to test whether the pass fills seats that would otherwise be empty, attracts paying guests, and earns enough to cover royalties and any ticket sales it replaces.

## What the pilot shows

| Month | Active passes | Pass-holder visits | Single tickets sold | Recorded admissions | Available seats | Seats filled | Visits per active pass |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| January | 80 | 180 | 940 | 1,120 | 2,000 | 56.0% | 2.25 |
| February | 95 | 250 | 880 | 1,130 | 1,840 | 61.4% | 2.63 |
| March | 105 | 205 | 1,020 | 1,225 | 2,100 | 58.3% | 1.95 |
| April | 112 | 280 | 865 | 1,145 | 1,750 | 65.4% | 2.50 |
| **Total** | **392 pass-months** | **915** | **3,705** | **4,620** | **7,690** | **60.1%** | **2.33** |

The table treats each single ticket sold as one admission. The active-pass total counts a pass once for each month it appears in the reported figures. It gives a denominator for average monthly use, while the number of distinct pass holders remains unknown.

Active passes rose from 80 to 112, a 40% increase. Pass-holder visits accounted for about one in five recorded admissions across the pilot and nearly one in four in April. Average use ranged from 1.95 to 2.63 visits per active pass per month. The monthly figures show that pass holders made substantial use of the benefit. They do not show whether that use was spread evenly across holders or concentrated among a small number of frequent visitors. That distinction matters because the cinema earns the same 100 units on each pass while paying royalties on every visit.

The cinema recorded 3,070 unfilled seats across the pilot, including 605 in April, the fullest month by percentage. April had fewer admissions than March and a higher fill rate because it offered 350 fewer seats. Monthly fill rates therefore reflect changes in the number of seats offered as well as changes in attendance. For the expansion decision, the relevant question is whether spare seats are available at screenings pass holders would choose to attend.

## What remains uncertain

Single-ticket sales fell from 940 in January to 865 in April, while pass-holder visits rose from 180 to 280. One possible explanation is that some people bought passes and used them for films they would otherwise have paid to see. Other explanations are also consistent with the figures. Programming changed each month, available seats varied, and the distribution of screenings across nights may have affected attendance. March had the highest single-ticket sales of the four months even as the number of active passes rose. The pilot has no comparison that isolates the effect of passes from those other changes. The 75-ticket decline between January and April cannot serve as an estimate of sales lost to the pass.

Pass use can affect ticket sales in two ways. A pass holder can replace a ticket they would personally have bought, even at a screening with empty seats. A pass reservation can also take a seat someone else would have bought at a popular screening. The cinema knows some screenings sold out, but it did not record their times. The board cannot tell which nights or programs were constrained, how many seats pass holders used at those screenings, or whether anyone tried to buy a ticket after seats were gone. A sold-out screening establishes that all available seats were taken. Evidence of turnaways or waitlist demand would help estimate how many additional tickets could have sold.

The volunteer survey suggests another possibility. Pass holders may create ticket sales by inviting friends. The survey does not establish how many friends bought tickets, how often that happened, or whether those friends would have attended anyway. The finding is worth testing because just a few genuinely additional paid visits per pass could materially change the economics. Counting all companions as sales generated by the pass would overstate that effect.

Four months also leave much of the annual commitment unobserved. Early use could reflect enthusiasm after purchase, and later use could shift with the calendar or the program. The active-pass counts give no reliable measure of renewals or of how long each holder had been using the pass. The cinema can evaluate the pilot’s observed usage and royalty costs now. A full-year assessment requires following buyers from purchase through expiration.

## Financial implications

Each single ticket brings in 9 units and incurs a 2-unit screening royalty, leaving 7 units before other costs. The pilot’s 3,705 single tickets thus generated 33,345 units in gross sales and 25,935 after their screening royalties, assuming each ticket incurred one royalty. The 915 pass-holder visits incurred another 1,830 units in royalties. Pass revenue for the period cannot be reconstructed from the active-pass counts. The cinema needs actual purchase and renewal records, including dates and amounts, to determine how much it collected and which annual obligations those sales created.

At the individual pass level, the 100-unit price covers 50 visits’ worth of screening royalties. Dividing the observed 915 visits by 392 active pass-months gives 2.33 visits per pass-month. If that rate held over an entire year, a pass would average about 28 visits, incur 56 units in royalties, and leave 44 units before any effect on single-ticket sales and before other costs. This is a planning scenario. It assumes the four-month usage rate continues across the year, including months with different films and schedules.

At 28 visits, each single-ticket sale lost reduces that 44-unit contribution by another 7 units. Six lost sales leave 2 units, and seven produce a 5-unit loss, before other costs. Each additional paid visit attributable to the pass adds 7 units on the same basis. For example, a pass holder who makes 28 visits, replaces eight paid admissions, and generates three additional paid admissions would contribute 9 units before other costs. The calculation counts the 2-unit royalty on every pass visit and uses the 7-unit ticket margin to value any change in paid admissions.

The board should therefore judge the pass against expected results under the existing season plan. An annual pass can cover its holder’s royalties while still reducing the cinema’s contribution if it replaces enough paid visits. Conversely, a pass that fills spare seats and brings paying guests can contribute financially even if the holder visits often. If extra bookings create measurable staffing, booking, or other operating costs, those costs belong in the expansion decision as well.

## Proposal for next season

Keep the annual price at 100 units and authorize an initial tranche of up to 20 additional passes above the April level of 112 active passes. Use April as a reference point for the size of the test. Twenty is a proposed limit on the initial commitment, chosen because the cinema lacks showtime data for a capacity-based estimate. At the observed average rate, those passes would add around 47 visits in a typical month. The booking records should show where those visits land. Before selling the tranche, the cinema should also define the terms that will apply for the full annual pass period and budget for the royalties through expiration.

Start collecting screening-level data when next season’s booking opens. Each screening record should include its date and time, program, seats available for sale, paid bookings, pass bookings, attendance, and whether and when it sold out. Record waitlist requests or turnaways when possible, along with canceled reservations and no-shows. Record pass purchases, renewals, and expirations separately, and use a consistent pass identifier to follow visit frequency over time. Where the booking system can link paid companion tickets to pass reservations, use that link to count companion attendance. A short follow-up question asking whether the guest would have come independently can inform a range of estimates for additional ticket sales.

Review the results after the first two months of the expanded season. Compare screenings with similar programs and time slots where possible, and examine busy screenings individually. For the financial review, project annual usage under several assumptions, including heavier use than the pilot average. Show the contribution under a range of estimates for ticket sales lost and gained. Give the board a view based on zero additional companion sales as well as a view that credits the portion supported by booking and survey evidence. Separately report whether recent sellouts produced waitlists or turnaways and how much pass use occurred at those screenings.

Release another tranche only if the contribution remains positive under a conservative set of assumptions and the screening records show room for additional use. If the first tranche leaves the board unsure how much paid demand is being displaced, maintain that sales limit while collecting more data. If pressure is concentrated on particular nights or programs, use that evidence to evaluate whether a future pass with explicit off-peak terms would fit the cinema’s schedule. Honor the terms of passes already sold.

The board should also track the community benefit it expects from the pass. If one goal is to help residents attend more regularly, report how many distinct holders use it, how usage is distributed, and how often holders report attending films they would otherwise have skipped. The board can then decide explicitly whether any financial shortfall is worth funding for that benefit. The decision at the end of the season should combine screening-level capacity, paid-ticket effects, and observed use over the annual term before the cinema commits to a larger rollout.
